title: Veranda Marvelli Company memorial book: neutralize six mixed-scan 1910 postcard fronts to their in-scan grey step-wedge, rescue the faint handwritten backs each the correct way, vectorize the family collection stamp, then data-merge one restored postcard per page into a press-ready keepsake book
grounding_note: Adapted from a real Upwork family-history photo-restoration brief (a private individual digitizing ~24 antique 1910 postcard photographs of a touring stage-magician company, wanting the photographic FRONT and the handwritten BACK of each delivered restored and legible for a printed memorial book and social media) and kept to a fictional world — no real person, brand, org, troupe, venue, or trademark is named. The magician and his company are laundered to the fictional 'Veranda Marvelli Company' with a fictional lead 'Aldo Marvelli'; the family members named in the transcriptions are invented; only geographic place names (Singapore, Rangoon, Penang) and the delivery platform (Upwork) are real and allowed. REPOSITIONED for connector reality AND to fix the killed original, which was two straight-line tonal chains on a SINGLE postcard with every restoration craft excluded (no cross-asset consistency, no triage, no authored endpoint — just brighten-front / contrast-back). The rebuild scopes the collection to a bounded worked chapter of SIX representative postcards (six fronts + six backs) and turns the loose 'deliver two files' into the artifact the client actually wants: a press-ready keepsake MEMORIAL BOOK, one restored postcard per page, produced by a genuine one-file-per-row InDesign data-merge. To make consistency checkable the way a real archival digitization job does, the client is modeled as having laid a photographic neutral grey step-wedge target (a plain unbranded neutral grey/step reference) on the scanner bed beside every card, so the scanner's per-scan colour error has a free in-frame neutral reference; the client also supplies a hand-authored single-record book-page .indd (NOT a convert_pdf_to_indd output) carrying live <<fields>> and THREE @-image columns (front photo, back inset, repeating family collection stamp), a roster CSV whose caption column holds the family's own verbatim transcriptions of each back (so legibility is delivered by restoration + the client's transcription, never by agent OCR), the twelve raw skewed scans, and a flat inked family collection stamp to be prepped and vectorized for the page colophon. The Adobe chain does the real work the brief rewards: neutralize every front to its own in-scan grey wedge so the whole book shares one archival white point, build one consistent authored warm-sepia tone across the monochrome fronts, rescue each faint back the correct way for its medium, vectorize the stamp after prep-before-trace, then merge one restored postcard per page and export the book.
one_line_ask: Restore a chapter of a 1910 magician-company postcard collection into a press-ready memorial book: neutralize six differently-scanned sepia fronts to the grey step-wedge each scan carries so the whole book reads as one matched archival set, decide per card how far to move white balance and exposure, give the monochrome fronts one consistent authored warm-sepia tone, rescue each faint handwritten back the way its medium needs, vectorize the family collection stamp, then data-merge one restored postcard per page against the client's transcription roster into a single keepsake-book PDF.
full_brief: A family-history client is digitizing a relative's collection of 1910 photographic postcards documenting the Veranda Marvelli Company, a stage-magic troupe that toured Southeast Asia, and wants them turned into a printed keepsake memorial book plus social posts. Each postcard is two things: a sepia photographic FRONT of the magician and company on stage, and a handwritten BACK where the client's grandmother described the scene. We are handing you a worked chapter of six postcards — the six fronts and their six backs — and everything the job needs; we are not reshooting or retyping anything. Here is the problem with the fronts: they were captured on a flatbed scanner across several sessions and they do not match — some are dark and low-contrast, some heavily yellowed, one is over-warm, one is flat and grey, and each scan carries a slightly different colour error from the scanner glass, so straight out of the folder the set looks like a jumble and a book of mismatched cards reads cheap. To make this checkable, whoever scanned them laid a photographic grey step-wedge (a neutral grey reference target) on the scanner bed beside every card. Your job on the fronts: bring every front to one consistent, true archival look by neutralizing each one to the grey wedge it carries — the wedge must read as a clean neutral grey (even across the channels) in your finished frame, and once every wedge is neutral the whole book shares one white point; then give the fronts one consistent warm archival sepia tone so the chapter feels like a single collection, while still recovering the crushed shadows where the company stands in stage-dark and taming any blown footlight. Do NOT push one blanket correction across all six — each was scanned differently and needs its own white-balance and exposure decision to land on the shared target, some warming, some cooling, some mostly an exposure rescue — and when you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each card and the final pixel size, so we can confirm the set is matched and that every front will still be sharp at book-print size. That last part matters: each front drops into a 150 x 110 mm photo window on the page, and at press resolution that window needs at least ~1772 x 1299 px of real image — a card cropped down small will print soft, which we will reject. Second, the backs: the handwriting is faint — some in brown ink, some in silvery pencil, one with a faint circular postmark we want kept — and it needs to be clearly legible in the book. Get each back clean and readable, but understand they are not the same problem and must not be treated the same way: the medium of each back decides how hard you can push. Third, our family collection stamp exists only as a flat inked impression on off-white paper — get it clean and razor-sharp so it can sit as a small colophon mark on every page. Finally, build the book: we have hand-built the InDesign page template with the real placeholder fields and three image slots (front photo, back inset, and the collection stamp), and we are giving you the roster with each card's plate number, place, date line, and the transcription of the back exactly as our grandmother wrote it; merge them so every postcard becomes its own book page — the restored front dropped in, the rescued back inset beside it, the transcription bound verbatim, and the stamp in the corner — then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI memorial-book PDF, one restored postcard per page. Bind the captions and plate data verbatim from the roster; do not rewrite or reorder anyone's words. Acceptance: every grey wedge neutral and the whole set on one archival white point; every front at least ~1772 x 1299 px so it prints >=300 DPI in the photo window; every back clearly legible for its medium with the postmark preserved; the collection stamp a clean crisp vector; and exactly one finished book page per roster row.

inputs.name: marvelli_memorial_book_template.indd
inputs.gen_prompt: AUTHORED DELIVERABLE (cannot be model-generated): a genuine, hand-built Adobe InDesign document (.indd/.idml) for a SINGLE-RECORD memorial-book PAGE (A4 landscape, 3 mm bleed) — ONE postcard per page. It must contain live InDesign data-merge placeholder fields <<PlateNo>>, <<Location>>, <<DateLine>>, <<Caption>>, and THREE @-prefixed image-path merge columns wired to three separate image frames: a 150 x 110 mm photo window bound to @Front (the restored front), a 70 x 50 mm inset window bound to @Back (the rescued handwritten back), and a small ~14 x 14 mm colophon window in the page corner bound to @Emblem (the vectorized family collection stamp). The <<Caption>> text frame has Auto-Size 'shrink text to fit' enabled so long transcriptions bind without going overset. The book's running title, folio and rule lines are already drawn into the template artwork (fixed on every page), so the only per-row imagery is the front, the back inset and the repeating stamp. Built by hand in InDesign so the merge fields and ALL THREE image fields actually bind. Explicitly NOT a convert_pdf_to_indd output: a converted-PDF template has no live merge fields and no data-merge image field, so it would not bind — which is exactly the defect this benchmark avoids.
inputs.realism_notes: document_merge_data_layout is [T] and REQUIRES a user-authored .indd carrying real merge fields plus genuine @image-path columns, and it emits ONE FILE PER ROW — so a single-record per-postcard book page is the correct, connector-doable shape (six rows => six pages => one book). Supplied as an input, not a chain output; a PDF-converted .indd with literal typed text would not bind. THREE image columns (@Front, @Back, @Emblem) mean the merge resolves three prepped assets per row — the row's restored front, its rescued back, and the shared vectorized stamp — giving the chain-produced vector stamp a real connector-doable path onto every page as a merge bind, never free-form placement. Column names must exactly match the roster headers.

inputs.name: marvelli_postcard_roster.csv
inputs.gen_prompt: Generate a CSV with headers exactly: PlateNo,Location,DateLine,Caption,@Front,@Back,@Emblem and 6 postcard rows (one per card in the worked chapter). PlateNo is 'Plate I' through 'Plate VI'. Location is a fictional-safe touring stop using real geography only: 'Grand Rialto, Singapore', 'Empire Hall, Penang', 'Gaiety Stage, Rangoon', 'Rialto Annexe, Singapore', 'Harbour Pavilion, Penang', 'Star Rooms, Rangoon'. DateLine is a month/1910 (e.g. 'March 1910'). Caption is the family's VERBATIM transcription of that card's back in a period first-person voice, each 1-2 lines, at least two of them deliberately LONG (e.g. 'Front row, my mother and Aunt Lillian with the whole Company at the Grand Rialto the night Mr Marvelli made the elephant vanish — Singapore, March 1910') so the template's shrink-to-fit is exercised; the transcription is SUPPLIED by the client, never produced by the agent. @Front holds the restored front filename for that row (front_01_final.jpg ... front_06_final.jpg, in row order). @Back holds the rescued back filename (back_01_final.jpg ... back_06_final.jpg). @Emblem holds the SAME vectorized stamp file — marvelli_collection_stamp.svg — in EVERY row, so the merge drops the one shared colophon mark onto every page as a merge bind. Column names must exactly match the template merge fields <<PlateNo>>,<<Location>>,<<DateLine>>,<<Caption>> and the three @image-path columns.
inputs.realism_notes: Six rows => the merge must produce exactly six book pages (page-count = row-count gate). The Caption column carries the client's own transcription verbatim, so legibility of the handwriting is delivered by the restoration PLUS the supplied transcription — never by agent OCR or any text-from-image read (which is not connector-doable and is banned). The @Front / @Back columns hold filenames the agent must produce and upload under those exact names, so naming discipline is a real dependency; @Emblem carries the identical SVG in all six rows, giving the vectorized stamp its connector-doable path onto every page. Long captions exercise the auto-fit frame.

inputs.name: raw_postcard_fronts_x6.zip
inputs.gen_prompt: A set of 6 REAL flatbed-scanner captures of 1910 photographic postcard FRONTS, each ~3500-4500 px on the long edge (full-resolution archival scans before crop), each with a photographic grey STEP-WEDGE (a photographic neutral grey step-wedge target, no brand or model name) laid flat on the scanner bed in one margin of the frame as a neutral reference, surrounded by the light-gray scanner-bed margin. All show the fictional Veranda Marvelli Company (a magician in tailcoat and about eight performers in early-1900s touring costume on a wooden theatre stage with painted backdrop and footlights), photoreal sepia/albumen monochrome with real emulsion grain, foxing and age. Deliberately MISMATCHED so no single correction fits: (1) dark, low-contrast, crushed stage-shadows, faint COOL/greenish scanner cast, tilted ~4 deg; (2) heavily YELLOWED/faded, washed highlights, level; (3) a genuine HAND-TINTED colour postcard — the same troupe but with period hand-applied colour (rosy cheeks, tinted costumes, blue-green backdrop), shot under near-neutral light so its grey wedge already reads neutral and the colour is REAL, tilted ~3 deg; (4) OVER-WARM orange cast, otherwise fine, tilted ~3 deg; (5) FLAT low-contrast neutral grey albumen, dull, level; (6) very DARK and underexposed, company lost in shadow, tilted ~4 deg. Each front has real film grain and paper texture, no modern sharpness, no CGI gloss; the grey step-wedge is clearly visible and uncropped in every frame.
inputs.realism_notes: REAL flatbed-scan captures at ~3500-4500 px long edge (NOT a ~1024-1536 px AI-gen raster) precisely so each crop fills the 150 x 110 mm photo window at ~300 DPI by DOWNSCALE ONLY — no upscaling anywhere. Deliberately mismatched (per-scan WB, exposure and tilt vary in opposite directions) so a single blanket correction cannot fix the set — each front needs its own decision measured to its in-scan grey step-wedge, the free checkable neutral target (inputs are generated, so the target costs nothing). Card 3 is the UNDISCLOSED TRAP: it is a genuine hand-tinted colour postcard whose grey wedge already reads neutral, so warming it toward sepia or forcing it into the monochrome tone strips the real hand-applied colour — the brief only says 'give the fronts one consistent warm sepia tone', so the naive agent tones all six. The grey wedge is cropped OUT of the final front; the pre-crop neutralized master (wedge in frame) is retained for grading.

inputs.name: raw_postcard_backs_x6.zip
inputs.gen_prompt: A set of 6 REAL flatbed-scanner captures of the BACKS of the same 1910 postcards, each rendered large (~2600-3400 px long edge) with a light-gray scanner-bed margin around the card. Each is a divided-back postcard printing (faint printed 'POST CARD' header, vertical divider, stamp box) with several lines of faint hand-written cursive describing the scene, aged cream/yellowed paper with foxing. Deliberately DIFFERENT media so the rescue is not one recipe: (1) faint BROWN INK cursive, low ink/paper contrast, tilted ~3 deg; (2) silvery GRAPHITE PENCIL cursive, very low contrast and easily crushed if over-pushed, tilted ~3 deg; (3) brown ink PLUS a faint circular smudged 1910 POSTMARK over part of the writing that must be kept readable, level; (4) brown ink with heavy orange FOXING spots and a soft stain across the text, tilted ~4 deg; (5) MIXED pencil-and-ink on one card, uneven density, tilted ~3 deg; (6) extremely FAINT washed ink, the hardest to read, level. Photoreal aged-paper texture, authentic period cursive, low contrast between mark and paper, no modern crispness.
inputs.realism_notes: gemini-3-pro-image chosen because the backs are TEXT-bearing (printed postcard layout + real cursive). Rendered at ~2600-3400 px so each rescued back downscales into the 70 x 50 mm inset window (~827 x 591 px floor) with no upscaling. The medium differences are the whole point: the brown-ink cards take a hard contrast push, the SILVERY PENCIL card (2) is crushed to nothing by that same hard push and needs a gentle contrast + tone, and card 3's faint postmark is destroyed by an aggressive black-point clip and must be protected — so 'make the backs legible' is a per-card divergent decision, not one blanket contrast slam. Legibility of the WORDS is carried by the client's verbatim transcription in the roster; the image rescue makes the actual handwriting readable in the inset. Scanner margin + tilt give the deskew/crop real work.

inputs.name: marvelli_collection_stamp_scan.png
inputs.gen_prompt: A flat desktop scan of a family archival COLLECTION STAMP inked on off-white textured paper: a small circular hand-inked impression reading 'THE MARVELLI FAMILY COLLECTION' around the rim with a simple central star-and-wand motif, deep ink on slightly warm off-white stock. Rendered as a real scan — the paper is a warm off-white (NOT transparent, NOT pure white), the impression sits very slightly rotated (~2 deg) on the scan bed, there is extra paper margin around the mark, ink is solid but edges are a touch soft as a real stamp impression would be. High enough contrast that, once cleaned, it will vectorize cleanly. Open, legible letterforms with clear gaps (no delicate enclosed counters relied on for a dark-ground knockout).
inputs.realism_notes: Scanned-on-paper (off-white ground, slight rotation, margin, soft edges) so image_vectorize would trace the paper and the skew if fed raw — forcing genuine prep-before-trace: straighten, crisp the contrast, crop to the mark, knock the off-white ground to transparency, THEN vectorize. It goes onto a LIGHT book page, so any counters that read as white after the crisp-to-white prep are fine (no dark-ground knockout is claimed). gemini-3-pro-image for clean legible lettering.

outputs.name: Marvelli_Memorial_Book_Chapter_x6.pdf
outputs.spec: One press-ready A4-landscape memorial-book PDF of exactly six pages — ONE restored postcard per roster row (page-count = row-count = 6) — exported from the one-file-per-row InDesign data-merge with 3 mm bleed at ~300 DPI; each page binds its PlateNo/Location/DateLine/Caption verbatim from the roster, drops that card's grey-wedge-neutralized restored front into the 150 x 110 mm photo window (via @Front, >=1772 x 1299 px so it prints >=300 DPI), the rescued handwritten back into the 70 x 50 mm inset (via @Back), and the vectorized family collection stamp into the corner colophon (via @Emblem, the same SVG every page) — all by merge bind, never free-form placement.

outputs.name: restored_fronts_x6
outputs.spec: Six grey-wedge-neutralized, deskewed restored postcard fronts, delivered as the photo-window crops (grey step-wedge cropped OUT) that bind into the book, alongside their RETAINED pre-crop neutralized masters (the *_neutralized full-res frames, step-wedge still in frame) which the harness keeps as the neutrality-grading artifacts. Acceptance (grader-checked, SEPARATE claims): (a) neutralisation is graded on the RETAINED pre-crop neutralized master of each front (its in-scan grey wedge still present) — the wedge region reads a clean neutral (per-channel spread near zero) with the whole set matched to one shared archival white point, shadows recovered and highlights held; the five monochrome fronts additionally carry one consistent authored warm-sepia tone, while the hand-tinted card (Plate III) KEEPS its real hand-applied colour (its wedge neutral but its colour NOT collapsed to sepia); (b) card-exclusion is checked separately on each delivered photo-window crop (grey wedge fully cropped OUT, no wedge pixels present) and each crop is >=1772 x 1299 px. Accompanied by a report of the final white-balance and exposure move AND the final pixel size for each front.

outputs.name: rescued_backs_x6
outputs.spec: Six rescued handwritten backs, each deskewed, edge-cropped and made clearly legible for ITS medium and converted to a clean high-legibility monochrome/sepia: the brown-ink cards pushed to hard ink/paper separation; the silvery graphite-pencil card (Plate II) rescued with a gentler contrast that keeps the pencil intact rather than crushed; the postmark card (Plate III) legible with its faint circular postmark preserved (no black-point clip that erases it). Each >=827 x 591 px for the 70 x 50 mm inset. Accompanied by a note of the contrast/tone move applied per back.

outputs.name: marvelli_collection_stamp.svg
outputs.spec: Clean vector SVG of the family collection stamp, traced only after the scan is straightened, crisped, cropped to the mark, and knocked to transparency — razor-sharp at the ~14 mm colophon scale with no captured paper ground or skew.

connector_workflow.note: Triage: this front sits ~4 deg crooked on the scanner bed, so level it before any tonal work. (Only the tilted fronts 1/3/4/6 get straightened; the level fronts 2/5 skip this — deciding which is part of the job.)

Dark, low-contrast, faint COOL/greenish scanner cast: WARM it (positive temperature) and set tint until the in-scan grey step-wedge reads neutral (R=G=B), then LIFT exposure and recover the crushed stage-shadows (shadows/blacks up) while holding any footlight highlight, so faces and stage detail read. Reason the exact temperature/exposure to THIS wedge — do NOT reuse another card's numbers. Report the final move. Single primitive-built adjustments call (replaces the deprecated image_adjust_color_temperature / _highlights / _brightness_and_contrast).

Authored archival TONE pass: now that the wedge is neutral, apply the one consistent warm-sepia tone the whole book will share (a controlled positive temperature/warm split toward amber in the mids, gentle contrast) — this is the agent-authored look, reasoned from primitives, NOT an image_apply_preset pick and NOT auto_tone. The SAME tone target is applied to every monochrome front (2/5/... ) so the chapter reads as one collection; the divergence lives in the neutralize pass, the convergence in this tone pass.

Crop the toned front to the 150 x 110 mm photo-window ratio, framing on the postcard image with the grey step-wedge cropped OUT — this wedge-removed crop binds into the book via @Front. The pre-crop neutralized master (front1_neutralized, wedge still in frame) is RETAINED as the neutrality-grading artifact; the wedge is graded THERE, never on this crop, and card-exclusion is the separate check on this crop. Keep >=1772 x 1299 px so it prints >=300 DPI. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only, never generative-expand. Report final px.

Level frame, heavily YELLOWED/faded with washed highlights: the dominant move is COOL/de-yellow (negative temperature) to bring its grey wedge to neutral, plus PULL the washed highlights down and add contrast to restore body. Opposite WB direction from front 1 — proof the batch is not uniformly cool. Report the move.
Apply the shared authored warm-sepia tone (same target as front 1) so this card matches the book. Monochrome front => gets the tone. Convergence step.
Crop the wedge out, reframe to the 150 x 110 mm photo window at >=1772 x 1299 px. Retain front2_neutralized as the grading master. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only. Report final px.
Tilted ~3 deg — level it. This is the hand-tinted card; straightening is geometry only and safe.

THE UNDISCLOSED TRAP CARD. Plate III is a genuine HAND-TINTED colour postcard shot under near-neutral light, so its in-scan grey wedge ALREADY reads neutral: the correct move is essentially NO white-balance shift — only match exposure/brightness to the set and hold. A naive agent that batch-applies the 'warm the cool cast' move used elsewhere, or reads the tint as a cast to remove, will push the wedge off-neutral and start killing the real hand-applied colour. Decision must be driven by THIS wedge, not the batch. Report that WB was held and colour preserved.

Crop the wedge out, reframe to the 150 x 110 mm photo window at >=1772 x 1299 px. CRITICAL: this card does NOT get the monochrome warm-sepia tone pass — its real hand-applied colour is the point, so the tone step (3/6/...) is deliberately SKIPPED for Plate III. Retain front3_neutralized as the grading master. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only. Report final px.
Tilted ~3 deg — level it.

OVER-WARM orange scanner cast: COOL it (negative temperature) until its grey wedge reads neutral, small exposure trim to match the set. A modest, careful correction — over-cooling would push it blue off the shared white point. Report the move.
Apply the shared authored warm-sepia tone. Monochrome front => gets the tone. Convergence.
Crop the wedge out, reframe to the 150 x 110 mm photo window at >=1772 x 1299 px. Retain front4_neutralized as the grading master. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only. Report final px.

Level frame, FLAT low-contrast neutral grey albumen: its wedge is already close to neutral, so only a SMALL WB nudge is needed — over-correcting pushes it off the set. The real work here is TONAL: add contrast and clarity to give the dull scan body without clipping. Report the (small WB, tonal) move.
Apply the shared authored warm-sepia tone. Monochrome front => gets the tone. Convergence.
Crop the wedge out, reframe to the 150 x 110 mm photo window at >=1772 x 1299 px. Retain front5_neutralized as the grading master. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only. Report final px.
Tilted ~4 deg — level it.

Very DARK and underexposed, company lost in shadow: the dominant move is a big EXPOSURE lift plus strong shadow/blacks recovery to pull the company out of the dark, THEN a WB nudge so its grey wedge lands neutral on the shared white point; protect any footlight from blowing. Tonal rescue dominates here — the largest exposure move in the set. Report the move.
Apply the shared authored warm-sepia tone. Monochrome front => gets the tone. Fronts 1/2/4/5/6 now share one neutral white point AND one authored sepia; Plate III holds its real colour. Convergence.
Crop the wedge out, reframe to the 150 x 110 mm photo window at >=1772 x 1299 px. Retain front6_neutralized as the grading master. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only. Report final px.
Begin the BACK chain. This back is tilted ~3 deg — level it before the legibility work. (Backs 1/2/4/5 are tilted and get straightened; backs 3/6 are level and skip it.)

Faint BROWN INK on cream, low contrast: push contrast HARD and set the black/white points so the ink separates cleanly from the paper — brown ink survives an aggressive push. This is the strong-push treatment; do NOT reuse its numbers on the pencil card. Report the move.
Convert to a clean high-legibility monochrome/sepia, killing the yellow paper cast and foxing colour so the handwriting reads as dark ink on clean ground for the book inset.
Crop the scanner margin off to the postcard edge and size to the 70 x 50 mm inset ratio at >=827 x 591 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only.
Tilted ~3 deg — level it.

TRIAGE DIVERGES: this back is SILVERY GRAPHITE PENCIL, very low contrast and easily crushed. The hard black-point push used on the brown-ink card would obliterate the pencil to nothing — instead use a GENTLE contrast lift with a raised black point (do not clip to pure black) plus a small exposure/clarity nudge so the faint pencil strokes strengthen without disappearing. Same goal (legible), different craft because the medium differs. Report the (gentle) move.
Convert to the clean monochrome/sepia inset look, matching the other backs while keeping the delicate pencil intact.
Crop the margin off and size to the 70 x 50 mm inset ratio at >=827 x 591 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only.

Level card, brown ink PLUS a faint circular smudged POSTMARK the client wants kept: push contrast to make the ink legible but HOLD the black point OFF pure black so the faint postmark is not clipped away — an aggressive clip erases the postmark. A protect-the-faint-detail treatment, distinct from the full-strength push on back 1. Report the move and that the postmark was preserved.
Convert to the clean monochrome/sepia inset look while keeping the postmark visible.
Crop the margin off and size to the 70 x 50 mm inset ratio at >=827 x 591 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only.
Tilted ~4 deg — level it.

Brown ink with heavy orange FOXING and a soft stain: push contrast to separate the ink, using exposure/whites to lift the stained ground toward clean paper without blowing the ink. The foxing colour is handled by the monochrome tint next. Report the move.
Convert to the clean monochrome/sepia inset look, which collapses the orange foxing colour to a uniform tone so only the handwriting reads.
Crop the margin off and size to the 70 x 50 mm inset ratio at >=827 x 591 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only.
Tilted ~3 deg — level it.

MIXED pencil-and-ink, uneven density: a MODERATE contrast lift that reads the darker ink without crushing the lighter pencil passages — a middle path between the hard-push and gentle-push cards. Report the move.
Convert to the clean monochrome/sepia inset look.
Crop the margin off and size to the 70 x 50 mm inset ratio at >=827 x 591 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only.

Level card, extremely FAINT washed ink — the hardest read: a strong exposure/whites lift on the paper plus a firm contrast push to bring the washed ink up, stopping short of clipping the thinnest strokes to nothing. Report the move. The six backs now read legibly, each rescued for its own medium.
Convert to the clean monochrome/sepia inset look.
Crop the margin off and size to the 70 x 50 mm inset ratio at >=827 x 591 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only.
Prep-before-trace step 1: the stamp scan sits ~2 deg rotated on the bed — straighten so the vector edges are square. Feeding the raw skewed scan to vectorize would bake in the rotation.

Prep-before-trace step 2: push contrast/clarity and drive the off-white paper toward clean white so the ink separates hard from the ground — a soft low-contrast scan traces into ragged, doubled edges.
Prep-before-trace step 3: crop away the scan margin to the tight bounds of the impression so vectorize traces only the stamp, not the paper field.

Prep-before-trace step 4: knock the off-white paper ground to transparency so the trace captures the inked impression only, not a rectangle of paper. remove_background -> transparency (NOT select->invert->fill). The mark goes onto a LIGHT book page, so open counters reading as white are fine — no dark-ground knockout is claimed.

Now trace the prepared raster (straightened, crisped, cropped, transparent) into a clean SVG for the page colophon. Tracing the raw scan instead would produce a skewed, paper-bounded, fuzzy silhouette — the trap this prep chain avoids.

connector_workflow.inputs_from: front_01_final, front_02_final, front_03_final, front_04_final, front_05_final, front_06_final, back_01_final, back_02_final, back_03_final, back_04_final, back_05_final, back_06_final, marvelli_collection_stamp.svg
connector_workflow.note: Initialize an upload session for the six restored fronts, the six rescued backs and the vector stamp so the merge can resolve them by the @Front, @Back and @Emblem columns. Files uploaded under the exact names the roster references.
Finalize the upload; returns the asset URNs the roster's @Front / @Back / @Emblem columns resolve to for each single-record book page.

One-file-per-row InDesign data-merge: bind each of the six roster rows (PlateNo/Location/DateLine/Caption) into the authored SINGLE-RECORD .indd's live <<fields>> and resolve ALL THREE image columns per row — drop that card's restored front into @Front, its rescued back into @Back, and the shared vectorized stamp into @Emblem — producing EXACTLY ONE merged page per row (six pages); the auto-fit caption frame shrinks the long transcriptions. [T] requires the hand-authored template. A convert_pdf_to_indd template or a multi-up sheet would not bind / cannot be produced — this is the corrected merge path, and the stamp reaches every page only as this @Emblem merge bind, never free-form placement.

Export the merged single-record pages to one press-ready ~300 DPI A4-landscape + 3 mm bleed memorial-book PDF, one restored postcard per page. document_render_layout exports the WHOLE merged multi-page document in a single call — it cannot pull one named page out as its own file, so the book is the whole set. Acceptance: page-count = row-count = 6; if fewer, the merge collapsed rows and failed.

chaining_note: Strict output-to-input chaining throughout, three converging streams. difficulty_rationale: Long-horizon flagship with difficulty from DEPTH, not plumbing: 52 connector calls, 11 distinct Adobe tools across three groups (image_* grade/prep/tint/vectorize, asset_* storage, document_* merge/export), far above the >=10 call / >=6 distinct-tool floor even after stripping the 2 upload steps and the conditional auto-straightens. The core is not a repeated recipe: each of the six front neutralizations is a DIFFERENT reasoned decision in a different direction (warm the cool, cool the yellowed and the over-warm, hold WB on the hand-tinted trap, small-WB+tonal on the flat, big-exposure rescue on the dark) all forced to converge on one measurable target — the in-scan grey step-wedge — and then a SECOND authored tone pass unifies the monochrome fronts to one warm-sepia while the tinted card is held out; the six back rescues likewise diverge by medium (a hard ink push would crush the pencil card and clip away the postmark, so pencil and postmark cards demand gentler, protective treatments). Every front crop must additionally clear a numeric print-DPI floor (>=1772 x 1299 px in the 150 x 110 mm window). Layered on top is a genuine prep-before-trace vectorize of a skewed off-white stamp scan and a THREE-image-column one-file-per-row data-merge into a hand-authored single-record book template that turns the loose 'two files per card' ask into a real designed keepsake book. hardness_rationale: FAILURE GATE (a wrong DECISION, not a self-measurement): every front carries a physical grey step-wedge in-scan and the acceptance criterion is that each finished wedge reads a clean neutral with the whole book matched to one archival white point — a target the agent can miss — and the agent must REPORT the final white-balance/exposure move AND final pixel size per front, so 'matched' and 'sharp' are verifiable rather than asserted; two further checkable gates back it: each front crop must clear >=1772 x 1299 px, and the merged book page-count must equal the roster row-count (6), since document_merge_data_layout is one-file-per-row. HUMAN-HARD ELEMENTS: (1) cross-asset neutralization of six differently-scanned fronts to a common measurable white point, each needing its own opposite-direction correction, followed by a converging authored warm-sepia tone the agent must build from primitives (not a preset, not auto_tone) — plus the numeric DPI floor on every front; (2) a medium-aware triage of six faint backs that require DIFFERENT correct rescues — the hard black-point push that reads the brown-ink cards would crush the silvery graphite-pencil card to nothing and clip away card III's faint postmark, so those demand gentler, detail-protecting treatments; (3) prep-before-trace discipline on a skewed, off-white, margin-padded stamp scan (straighten -> crisp -> crop-to-bounds -> knock-to-transparency) before vectorize. UNDISCLOSED TRAP: the brief asks only for 'one consistent warm archival sepia across all the fronts' and never says one card is different — but Plate III is a genuine HAND-TINTED colour postcard whose grey wedge already reads neutral, so the naive path warms it and runs it through the monochrome sepia tone like the rest, silently destroying the real hand-applied colour; the correct path inspects, holds white balance, and skips the tone pass for that one card. A second pitfall sits in the merge (a convert_pdf_to_indd or multi-up template will not bind — only the supplied single-record authored .indd merges) and a third in the backs (a blanket hard-contrast slam crushes the pencil and erases the postmark). MEASURABLE ACCEPTANCE (decoupled so no artifact is graded on a region it crops away): (a) grey wedge neutral (per-channel spread near zero) and the set on one white point, evaluated on the six RETAINED pre-crop neutralized masters (wedge still in frame), with the five monochrome fronts on one authored sepia and Plate III's real colour preserved; (b) card-exclusion checked separately on the six delivered photo-window crops (wedge cropped OUT) each >=1772 x 1299 px; (c) each back legible for its medium with the postmark preserved and each >=827 x 591 px; (d) the stamp a clean skew-free transparent-ground vector; (e) exactly one press-ready ~300 DPI book page per roster row; plus the agent's reported per-card WB/exposure and back contrast params.
